Slipping ratings, a revolving door of lead actors, and nothing quite hitting like that old school David Tennant run. It’s dog days for “Doctor Who” fans, whose lives aren’t likely to be made any better by the prospect of AI creeping into the show.

While speaking at the Royal Television Society conference in London, BBC director Matt Brittin extolled the amazing efficiency of using AI to crank out footage — before raising the possibility of using it on one of the British broadcaster’s most beloved series.

“Everyone’s got the ability in their hands — or six billion people have — to create content at the standard of a Hollywood studio,” Brittin said, as quoted by Variety .

“Somebody sent me a 50-minute episode of ‘Doctor Who’ that was AI-generated the other day. It’s pretty good,” he continued. “I mean, it’s not going to replace humans, and we’ll come on to that. So everyone’s a creator.”

Brittin, it’s worth noting, was president of Europe, Middle East, and Africa operations at Google — a major purveyor of AI tech — before joining the BBC .

You have to wonder what Brittin’s idea of “pretty good” is. Attempts at using AI to crank out a movie or short film have invariably produced low grade slop . While the tech can sometimes create realistic images or scenes in isolation, cobbling together disparate, screensaver-worthy images together doesn’t constitute an episode of hit television.

There’s a reason that filmmakers and other artists have turned their noses up at AI , along with the small matter of the tech threatening to drive them out of their jobs, and the fact that it was trained on their artwork and performances without permission. The ones that do use it get are often lampooned as hacks, has-beens or sellouts .

And for “Doctor Who,” a show that’s sputtering along on its 41st season and is currently on hiatus as it searches for new ideas, the last thing it needs at this creatively critical impasse is the injection of a tool that recycles old ideas without direction and rigidly conforms to bland aesthetics.

Though Brittin insisted that AI isn’t going to “replace humans,” he could barely disguise his belief that it soon will.

“Not all the creativity is bad,” he said of AI. “In some cases it’s not perfect but look at what you can do and that’s changing all the time,” he added, per Deadline .

Companies and organizations around the world would do well to accept what their new roles are in our current AI-driven paradigm: glorified target practice for rogue AI agents.

The latest of such cybersecurity incidents, which frontier AI labs have been happy to turn into public spectacles, comes from OpenAI. On Tuesday, the ChatGPT-maker apologized after its AI agents hacked their way into several Australian government websites. The most alarming of these cases, which took place in June, involved the autonomous AI systems accessing a database for Medicare, the country’s universal health insurance scheme.

It should all be water under the bridge, though, because OpenAI kindly set an email wishing the Australian government the “best” — a whole three months after the hacks took place.

Here’s what that email looked like, as shared by ABC AI reporter Cam Wilson on LinkedIn .

“We are notifying you of a security vulnerability identified during our review of OpenAI Model activity…” the communiqué began. “An OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password.”

“It was able to access this to read portions of internal program files and settings, obtain a list of files, and create and read back a small test file on the server,” it explained. “Our review found no evidence that the model accessed patient-level records, personal information or credentials; deleted data; or established ongoing access.”

It then recommended “that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it.”

“We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available,” the email concluded, before signing off. “Best, OpenAl Security Team”.

It would be an absurd email to send in any other context. Would a burglar who broke into your house and nosed through your family photos sending a letter assuring he didn’t steal anything — and recommending the head of the house to change the locks — help you sleep better at night?

The company was all apologies in its announcement posted Monday, vowing that it will do whatever it takes to “rebuild trust with the Australian people.” That will likely prove easier said than done.

Internet sleuths have dug up old posts that appear to belong to Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic employee who kicked the AI safety movement into overdrive with his sensational claim that the tech “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Coxon’s current X account, @hilbertspaess, was created in 2026, but the gumshoes found that there were two previous accounts on that platform under the same handle between 2021 and 2024. The first account has undergone several different display names. But its first name, as far back as November 2021, appears to be “Jacob Coxon,” ">archived data shows . The evidence linking the second account made in 2023 to Coxon is more tenuous, but appear to be written in the same style and cover the same topics as the first. (One of the detectives compiled the tweets into an easily searchable database here .)

Given Coxon’s drum-beating about AI’s supposed existential risks to humankind, observers have paid particular attention to the account’s posts on climate change, something that poses a definite existential risk — not just to humans but all life on the planet — and, of course, is scientifically verified and already underway.

Tell that to Coxon, though.

“it’s literally 2020 already. look at climate change headlines from the 1970s then look around. nothing is happening, use your eyes,” the account ">wrote in March 2022.

People who are “worried about climate change,” the account ">opined , are “beyond reason.” Perhaps if the planet gets hotter, there might be “positive consequences.”

“why it all gotta be bad?” the account wondered.

While some of the posts are clearly trollish in nature, they betray sincere skepticism of climate change’s importance.

“you shouldn’t even want to save the rainforest. the rainforest is a festering pit,” the account ">seethed . “nature is constantly screaming. animal are being tortured and eaten alive,” it added, before adding this zinger: “the rainforest is gay.”

“stopppp talking about ‘climate change’ pleasse,” it also begged.

There was also, for good measure, an apparent incredulous allusion to the Jewish death toll in the Holocaust.

“six million is a palpable taunt,” the ">tweet read, displaying a hallmark of Holocaust denialism.

We reached out to Coxon to comment on the posts and to confirm whether they were his, but didn’t hear back.

Coxon’s post last month claiming that the AI industry was “gambling with our lives” blew up to an extraordinary degree. He was far from the first “whistleblower” or AI figure claiming that the tech could kill us all, but his claims resonated around the world, from Silicon Valley to Capitol Hill, providing fresh ammo for AI safety experts sounding the alarm.

Almost immediately, top AI figures, including Elon Musk, Dario Amodei, and Sam Altman, sprang into action to declare the need for an AI slowdown, with lawmakers echoing their calls. Not much later and Amodei, Altman, and other AI leaders were in the White House with president Trump, signing an AI safety pact . There has probably never been so much urgency shown for climate change at an official level.

Almost immediately after his post went mega-viral (it’s now sitting at over 800,000 likes), Coxon went on Fox News and down played climate change.

“I agree with president Trump’s tweet that global warming doomsday scenarios were overplayed,” he told Fox’s Sean Hannity. “It’s a very slow process. We’re talking about doomsdays — completely absurd.”

“Many other catastrophic panics in the past have been just fearmongering,” he added. “The reason this is unique is AI is moving so incredibly quickly, we won’t have time to respond to it before it’s too late.”

Robert F. Kennedy Jr. doesn’t trust human doctors, but he does trust AI chatbots — and so should you, he’s using his authority as chief medical spokesperson in the US government to tell the public.

The crux of the health secretary’s recent remarks during his “fireside chat” with vice president JD Vance at the Make America Healthy Again Conference on Tuesday was that AI models are now “better informed” than physicians, empowering ordinary Americans to second guess what their doctor tells them at every turn. AI, he proclaimed, has the power “to free us from medical tyranny,” the New York Times reported .

It’s not an unsurprising line from a man whose distrust of scientific medicine stems from the fact that it disagrees with his crank health beliefs , which range from vaccine “skepticism” to promoting a red meat heavy diet. What’s more illuminating is how the Kennedy scion is explicitly touting AI as a way of undermining the medical establishment.

“One of the things that is going to change is that we’re never ever again going to be able to be dominated by public officials who tell us, ‘Trust the experts,'” Kennedy said, as quoted by the NYT .

“If somebody tells you, ‘Masks work, trust the experts,’ AI may tell you otherwise,” he continued. “If somebody tells you, ‘Social distancing works, trust the experts,’ AI may correct that. And if somebody tells you that a vaccine will prevent transmission and infection, or you need to take it to protect your grandmother, AI may say it actually doesn’t do that.”

At one point, Kennedy claimed that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had personally told him that it would be “malpractice for a doctor to make a diagnosis or make a prescription without at least checking AI.”

Many doctors, it’s true, do use AI tools for taking clinical notes, transcribing patient visits, and even looking up symptoms. One widely used medical AI tool called OpenEvidence is already used by around two thirds of physicians in the US, according to its internal data.

But there’s still significant skepticism over the reliability of these tools among actual medical professionals. A recent paper which concluded, like Kennedy, that AI models were surpassing human doctors drew significant criticism , including from the head of the American Medical Association. The AI scribes that many doctors use, meanwhile, have been caught making up nonexistent medical issues .

Even more worrying is the sycophancy of the AI chatbots that RFK wants Americans to be consulting. The AI industry has worked to make its models less overly agreeable amid numerous controversies over its chatbots allegedly driving some users to suicide, but with enough needling and persistence, someone looking to an AI model to confirm their beliefs can get it to do just that. (A golden example: “urine therapy” practitioners who believe in the healing powers of drinking your own pee have found an ally in AI models, which they’ve egged into reassuring themselves that their pseudoscientific beliefs are in fact completely sound .)

The upshot is that by peddling AI, Kennedy is eroding what little trust that Americans have left in our health institutions — trust that Kennedy, with his peddling of anti-vaccine rhetoric, has had a mighty hand in whittling down in the first place.

Rather than turning to experts for advice and trusting scientific consensus, AI will fragment us into increasingly niche sets of beliefs that are disconnected from reality. And with their proclivity for brown-nosing and making up facts, AI chatbots will exacerbate medical neuroses, trapping people in a cycle of distrust and unaddressed health issues. If you thought that crank health beliefs were bad now, imagine how much worse it will get as medical institutions are continually defunded and undermined — right as AI will tell them whatever quack advice they want to hear.
